note: Adam named first—not as a hero, but as the one through whom sin entered the world. Yet in Jesus, a second Adam came to undo what the first broke. That's how God reads the family tree.
Seth, chosen in Adam's place. The genealogies skip over Cain's line—God sees the faithful ones, not the proud. These names trace a thread of faith reaching toward the promise.
Enoch walked with God and was taken. Methuselah's long life spanned the faith of Noah's grandfather. Even when the world grew wicked, God kept a line of witnesses.
Noah saved through the flood, his three sons become the seed of all nations. God didn't destroy His people—He preserved them. From one faithful man, the whole earth was repeopled.
Japheth's sons settled in the northward lands—the Gentile nations. The family tree spreads outward; God's plan has always been wider than Israel alone.
Gomer and Togarmah—names that trace into the distant peoples. God sees them all by name, even before nations form and borders shift.
Javan, Tarshish, Kittim—names of seafaring peoples and trade routes. The chronicle shows how God's family scatters across the whole earth.
Ham's sons include Egypt, Ethiopia, and Canaan—nations vital to Israel's story. Some will be enemies, others neighbors; all are in God's sight.
Sheba and Dedan—the trader-names of Arabia. The genealogy isn't just names; it's the memory of peoples and their lands, all woven into one family story.
Nimrod 'began to be mighty'—first hunter, first to build the tower of Babel. When pride grows, God scatters. His power alone is lasting.
Mizraim fathered Egypt—land of plagues and slavery where Israel's story will be tested and refined. Every name holds a chapter of God's unfolding purpose.
The Philistines came from Casluhim—those who will harass Israel for generations. Yet even enemies are part of the record, part of how God shapes His people through struggle.
Sidon—Canaan's firstborn, an ancient city. Its people will trade, build, and later meet the prophets. Every name carries the weight of generations to come.
The Amorite, the Jebusite—peoples Israel will face as enemies in Canaan. They too came from Noah's line; they too could have chosen the Lord's way.
The Hivite, the Arkite—tribal names that will mark battles and boundaries. God knows each one; they matter to His story even when their names fade from memory.
Arvadite, Zemarite, Hamathite—coastal and inland peoples, merchants and warriors. The genealogy frames the map of all Israel will inherit.
Shem's sons lean eastward—Asshur, Aram, the heartland of the Middle East. From Shem comes Abraham's line; the elect run through this branch.
Arpachshad → Shelah → Eber. These links reach forward: Eber is father of Peleg, who will see the earth divided at Babel. Long chains of purpose, held fast by God.
Peleg—'the earth was divided' in his days. Babel's confusion, yet God chose one man's line through which the promise would flow unbroken.
Joktan and his sons spread toward Arabia. Even those who diverge from the main line of promise are held in God's memory, seen by His eye.
More names of Arabia's peoples, merchants and desert dwellers. The genealogy spans the known world—God's purposes embrace all nations.
Ophir's name will later echo as a land of gold and treasure. Names carry their meanings through time; God weaves all stories into one tapestry.
'All these were the sons of Joktan'—a summary pause. Even lines that don't lead to Israel are honored in the record. God misses no one.
Now the thread narrows—Shem's descendants in their order. The chronicle begins to follow the line of the covenant more closely, step by step toward Abraham.
Eber, Peleg, Reu—names of patience and duration. Each lived and waited; each passed the promise to the next. Faith waits; it does not rush.
Serug, Nahor, Terah—the line tightens. Terah will carry his son Abram from Ur; the promise moves nearer with each generation named.
Abram—also called Abraham. The name change marks a threshold: he is renamed in covenant, called to be father of nations. From here, the genealogy becomes the covenant family.
Isaac and Ishmael—both sons of Abraham, yet Isaac carries the promise forward. Both matter; not all children of the flesh are children of the covenant.
Ishmael's firstborn, Nebaioth—his line receives honor in the record, even though the covenant flows through Isaac. God blesses both, though the promise goes one way.
Kedar—later a name for Arabian peoples. Even those outside the covenant line are numbered and remembered; God sees and honors all His creatures.
'These are the sons of Ishmael'—a summary. The blessing spreads wide; the covenant thread stays narrow and sure, bound for Israel.
Keturah's sons—Abraham, though old, still fathers more. His fruitfulness echoes the promise; offspring like stars, though the covenant line is singular.
Midian—later a nation Israel will meet in the wilderness and at Judges' courts. Abraham's grandchildren spread across the lands where God will later work.
Abraham → Isaac; Isaac → Esau and Jacob (Israel). The narrowing continues. Jacob is renamed 'Israel'; from him the twelve tribes and the covenant people.
Esau's sons—he chose the earthly promise over the spiritual. His line becomes Edom, rival and neighbor to Israel; both brothers' descendants will fill the earth.
Eliphaz's children include Amalek—later Israel's archetypal enemy. From Esau's line comes one who will test Israel's faith and courage for generations.
Reuel's sons continue Esau's line. All named, all real; the genealogy honors Edom even as it traces the covenant through Jacob.
Seir the Horite—the peoples of the hill country before Israel enters. Geography and genealogy twine together; the land itself was inhabited.
Timna was Lotan's sister—the chronicle names both men and women, honoring how relationships bind families. Every person has a place in God's story.
Shobal and Zibeon's descendants fill the early Edomite lands. These names anchor a region where Esau's children made their home.
Anah fathered Dishon—genealogies are chains, each link in place. The specificity honors the reality that God works through real, named, interconnected people.
Ezer and Dishan's sons—more names of Edom's clans. Every valley and tribe in that land had fathers and families; all are written down before God.
Kings reigned in Edom 'before any king reigned over the children of Israel.' Edom organized under monarchy first; Israel would follow later, shaped by its own covenant.
Kings rise and fall in Edom, each remembered in turn. Human kingship is brief; the kingdom of God endures forever.
Husham of the Temanites—the cycle continues. One king dies, another takes the throne. Yet through it all, Israel's God is building toward His purpose.
Hadad struck Midian in Moab's field. Edom's kings wage wars; the land is contested. God's people will later know this same struggle.
Samlah of Masrekah—each name a dynasty, each king a chapter in Edom's story. None of their great deeds saves them from the grave.
Shaul of Rehoboth—a kingdom by the river, a city named. Power and possession pass like morning mist.
Baal Hanan—the name carries hints of false gods; still, even kings who chase idols are numbered in the record. God's patience is longer than any reign.
Hadad reigned again; his wife named Mehetabel. Even marriages and dynasties are briefly sketched. Life unfolds in names; eternity belongs to God alone.
'Then Hadad died.' The turning point: kings end, and chieftains rise. Edom's glory shifts from centralized rule to tribal leaders.
Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon—Edom's chiefs, each commanding a region. Power disperses; authority scatters among the clans.
Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar—more chiefs, more territories. Each name holds land and people; each is a thread in the tapestry Edom weaves.
Magdiel, Iram—the final chiefs of Edom. Readers today hear an echo in these names: all kingdoms rise and pass away, save One. Every genealogy points toward the King who never dies.

The chronicler names the twelve sons of Israel—not by their own strength, but as the Lord's chosen family. Notice how he keeps the lineage in order, showing us that genealogies matter in God's kingdom.

Readers today hear an echo in this genealogy: the Lord does not forget. In a world where names are lost and stories are erased, this chapter proclaims that God remembers every life, every covenant-keeper, every child of His promise. We, too, are written in His book.
Six more sons complete the list—and in them are all the tribes that will carry God's covenant into the future. Each name represents a family that God will work through in ways they never imagined.
Here we see Judah's sons through a Canaanite woman, yet the record does not shy from the judgment: Er was wicked, and the Lord took him. Even in the chosen line, God's justice is swift and true.
Tamar, a daughter-in-law who had to demand justice, bore the sons that carried the Davidic line. Sometimes the Lord works through a woman's quiet courage when men look away.
From Perez—whose name means "breaking through"—came Hezron and Hamul. The Lord often chooses names that point to His purposes: even a breach can become a blessing.
Zerah's line included men of renown—Ethan, Heman—whose names appear in the Psalms as wise men and singers. In God's house, musicians and thinkers have their place.
Achar earned the name "troubler of Israel"—his theft of devoted things brought judgment on all his people. One person's betrayal of covenant can reach far beyond their own life.
A single son, Azariah, carries forward the line of Ethan. Sometimes the narrowest branch proves crucial to God's design.
From Hezron came three sons: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai. The Lord divides inheritances so that multiple branches bear witness to His care.

Through Ram came Amminadab, Nahshon (a prince), Salma, Boaz, and Obed. In this line walks Boaz—a man of honor who loved a foreigner with covenant kindness. These are links in the chain that leads to David, and through David to the King of kings.

Jesse was the father of seven sons, but the seventh one—David—was the least valued. The Lord often chooses the overlooked one, the one tending sheep while others gathered at the feast. From the youngest, the anointed king came.
David's sisters, Zeruiah and Abigail, mothered men of war and wisdom. In God's economy, a woman's strength often shapes the strength of her sons—and the chronicler records her name with honor.

Caleb married twice: first Azubah, then Ephrath. His life spans generations and journeys; he knew the Lord's faithfulness across decades. After loss, he loved again—a quiet picture of resilience in God.
From Hur came Uri, and from Uri came Bezalel—the master craftsman who built the Tabernacle. God's artisans carry His vision just as prophets do.
Hezron took a wife at sixty years old and became a father still. The Lord's mercies are new each morning; age does not close the door to new chapters.
Jair possessed twenty-three cities in Gilead. The inheritance of names and lands reminds us that God's promises extend through generations, each one building on what the Lord gave their fathers.
Territories shift between hands; Geshur and Aram reclaimed towns Jair had held. Nothing we hold is truly ours to keep—the Lord gives and takes according to His will.
After Hezron died, his widow bore a son—Ashhur. Even in death, a man's name continues through those left behind, and the Lord sustains the family through sorrow.
Jerahmeel, the firstborn, received five sons—Ram, Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah. The firstborn's inheritance was often the heaviest; bearing a great name carried great responsibility.
Jerahmeel took another wife, Atarah, and she became mother to Onam. A second marriage can bring new blessings; the Lord does not measure love by the first chapter only.

The sons of Ram—Maaz, Jamin, and Eker—appear only in genealogy, yet the chronicler records their names. Every person who walked with the Lord is remembered in His sight, known or unknown to the world.
Onam fathered Shammai, who fathered Nadab and Abishur. The chronicler is careful to trace these lines—not to glorify them, but to show that God remembers the seed of covenant keepers.
Abihail bore Abishur's sons—Ahban and Molid. A wife's name and children are recorded here as part of the covenant line. Women are not incidental in God's record of His people.
Seled died without children, yet his brother Appaim continued the line. When one branch ends, another grows—God's covenant is not fragile; it endures.
Through Ishi, Sheshan, and Ahlai, the line continued unbroken. Simple names, quiet lives—yet they carried forward the promise their ancestors knew.
Jether died childless, but his brother Jonathan's sons—Peleth and Zaza—kept the family living. The Lord raises up others when one generation cannot bear children.
The sons of Jonathan are counted among the sons of Jerahmeel. In God's family, lineage is not erased; every name belongs to the whole people, and the whole people belongs to God.

Sheshan had no sons, only daughters—and so he gave his daughter to his Egyptian servant Jarha. Sometimes the Lord breaks convention to fulfill His design; a servant became family through an act of trust.

The long chain continues—Attai, Nathan, Zabad, and onward through Jekamiah to Elishama. Each generation heard the promise from the one before, carrying it forward like a lamp passed from hand to hand. The Lord's covenant transcends any earthly boundary.
Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel had sons who fathered towns—Mesha and Mareshah founded Ziph and Hebron. A man's name and his works often live on in the land itself.
The sons of Hebron—Korah, Tappuah, Rekem, and Shema—each carried a father's hope into their own generation. The strength of one man's faith ripples through his children.
Shema fathered Raham, Rekem fathered Shammai. The chronicler traces not just straight lines but the branching tree—showing how God's people spread and multiply across the land.
Shammai became father of Maon, who founded Beth Zur. In biblical genealogy, a man and his city often become one—he builds a place, and his name lives there forever.
Ephah, Caleb's concubine, bore three sons: Haran, Moza, and Gazez. In a household, all are counted—the chronicler's pen did not favor one wife's children over another's.
Jahdai's sons—Regem, Jothan, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph—are named, though we know nothing more of them. The Lord knows each one; fame does not measure a person's worth in His eyes.
Maacah, another of Caleb's concubines, bore Sheber and Tirhanah. A man's lineage grew through many women; in this, we see both human fragility and God's faithfulness to bless despite it.
Maacah bore three more sons and a daughter—Achsah. In this genealogy, the daughter's name is preserved as carefully as any son's. Women's names matter in God's record.
Caleb, son of Hur, fathered Shobal—and Shobal's name means "flowing"—founder of Kiriath Jearim. In genealogy, a name often hints at character or calling; the Lord gives names that fit.

Salma fathered Bethlehem—the very city where the Line of Judah would culminate in a Savior's birth. A founder's name became inseparable from his city; generations later, that city bore witness to Christ.
Shobal's son Haroeh lived in the Menuhoth, a place name meaning "rest." Even in genealogy's dry branches, we catch hints of the peace God gives to those who trust Him.
The families that came from Kiriath Jearim—Ithrites, Puthites, Shumathites, Mishraites—multiplied and spread. From one ancestor, many clans arose, each carrying the covenant seed.
The sons of Salma included Bethlehem and the Netophathites. These places and people, recorded here in a genealogy, became centers where God's word dwelt and witnesses lived.
The families of scribes at Jabez—the Tirathites, Shimeathites, Sucathites—were Kenites descended from Hammath. Scribes kept records, preserved words, wrote God's law; their labor was sacred work.

David's firstborn sons are set down by name and mother—each child a real person, not a cipher. Notice how the chronicler honors both son and mother, anchoring them in place: Amnon of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess. The Lord sees each child born, and so do we.

Absalom is named here as David's third son—the young man who would one day rise against his father. In this moment, though, he is simply listed: a child of Maacah, daughter of a foreign king. The Lord knew his end before his beginning.

The fifth and sixth sons complete the Hebron count. Eglah is named as David's wife here—a faithful presence in the record. Even in genealogy, the Lord honors the quiet faithfulness of those who stood beside the king.

Seven years and six months in Hebron; thirty-three in Jerusalem. These numbers frame David's reign in two halves—anointing in the south, then the capital secured in the north. The Lord measured his days in seasons.

Solomon is born in Jerusalem—son of Bathshua (called Bathsheba in other places). Here again, the chronicler names the mother alongside the children. From a union born in shadow came a son who would build the Lord's house. Grace works in ways we do not always see at first.

Three more sons, each with his own thread in the tapestry. Eliphelet appears twice in this listing—a name that echoes, yet points to different men. Even in a simple list, the Lord's people multiply and branch.

Three more sons, names bright and particular. Nogah means 'shining'; Nepheg, 'sprout.' Even in genealogy, the Lord's naming shows care—each child a gift, each name a small prayer spoken over his life.
Nine sons born in Jerusalem—a full number, a sign of blessing. Yet not all of them walked quietly into what the Lord had for them. Some would stumble; the Lord's grace would reach them still.
Tamar is named here—David's daughter, sister to all these sons. Her presence in the record matters; the chronicler will not let her fade. In a house of men, the Lord honors the daughters too.

Solomon's line begins: Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa, Jehoshaphat—a chain of kings stretching forward from David's son. Yet not all of them walked faithfully. The throne is passed, but it does not guarantee the heart.
Joram, Ahaziah, Joash—the line continues. Some of these kings would do what is right; others would turn their faces from the Lord. Yet still He did not abandon the covenant with David.

Amaziah, Azariah, Jotham—three more names in the succession. Azariah (also called Uzziah) would reach great strength, then pride would bring him low. The Lord's mercy endures even when we forget our need for Him.

Ahaz, Hezekiah, Manasseh—each a reign, each a test. Hezekiah especially sought the Lord's face in desperate hour; Manasseh would stumble into grave darkness before finding his way home. Even a king cannot hide from grace.

Amon, Josiah—the line moves toward exile. Josiah will be the last good king of Judah, and after him, the kingdom fractures. Yet even in the shadow of coming judgment, the Lord's faithfulness does not waver.

Four sons of Josiah are named—Johanan first, then Jehoiakim, Zedekiah, Shallum. None of them will inherit undivided peace. Yet the Lord sees each son, each struggle, each attempt to hold the kingdom together.

Jehoiakim's line—Jeconiah, who will be called the captive. The names grow heavier now; we feel the weight of exile drawing near. Yet the Lord does not abandon His covenant even when His people are carried away.

Shealtiel, son of Jeconiah the captive—this name marks a turning. Shealtiel means 'I have asked God.' In exile, a child is born; hope begins to stir again. The line does not end; it bends toward home.

Five sons of Jeconiah the captive are named—sons born into exile, yet sons nonetheless. Shenazzar especially will have a role to play in the return. Even captivity does not silence the Lord's purposes.

Zerubbabel emerges—the one who will lead the return and lay the temple's foundation anew. Shelomith is named as his sister; her place is kept in the record. The Lord honors the faithful, whether they stand in the temple's light or in the shadow.
Five grandsons of Zerubbabel—the line multiplies again in exile's aftermath. Each name represents a family continuing, a thread still held. The captivity is not the end; it is a turn in the road.

The genealogy spreads into branches—Hananiah's line, Rephaiah's, Arnan's, others. These names may be less known, yet each represents a family that continued the faith through exile and return. Faithfulness often wears a humble face.

Shecaniah's son Shemaiah, and his six sons—the line still branches. Six sons means blessing; they will become fathers and grandfathers themselves. The Lord's people multiply even when history forgets their names.

Neariah's three sons close out one branch. Three sons, three carriers of the name forward. How many of David's line survived the exile? Only the Lord knows; yet enough to fulfill His promise, and enough to lead us toward the Messiah.

Seven sons of Elioenai—a full number again, blessing renewed. Readers today hear an echo: through all the exile, all the forgetting, all the years when it seemed the covenant had broken, the Lord held fast. His line endured. That should comfort us now.

Here begin the sons of Judah—Perez, Hezron, and the rest who carry forward the tribe's name and calling. These names mark the long line that leads, generations down, to David and then to the Messiah himself. The Lord doesn't forget a name or a promise.

Reaiah and his descendants settle in Zorah, building families and homes in the Promised Land. Each generation inherits not just a name but a calling to dwell where the Lord has placed them. Faithfulness often looks like simply staying, tending what God has given.

Among the sons of Etam, note Jezreel and Idbash—and their sister Hazzelelponi, whose name means 'shade of my eye.' Even in a genealogy, she is named and remembered, valued by her household. The Lord sees the quiet ones, the ones who tend home and heart.

Penuel and Ezer—sons of Hur the firstborn of Ephrathah—are the fathers of Gedor and Hushah. Yet there is another Hur remembered here: the one who held up Moses' arms at Rephidim. Through generations, God weaves together families and faithfulness. Bethlehem itself is called Ephrath elsewhere in Scripture, a place the Lord would hold dear.

Ashhur and his two wives, Helah and Naarah, remind us that ancient life was complex—plural marriages existed in those days, though not without their own sorrows and tensions. The Lord met people where they stood and has never stopped doing so.

Naarah bore four sons: Ahuzzam, Hepher, Temeni, and Haahashtari—each one a blessing in her household. She is remembered by name and by her fruit. A mother's faithfulness in raising children echoes through generations, even when the world forgets her.

Helah's three sons—Zereth, Izhar, and Ethnan—are named and recorded, part of the great tapestry God is weaving. Each name, each life, matters in His sight, whether or not we remember them thousands of years later.

Hakkoz fathered Anub and Zobebah, and Aharhel through them. Again the genealogy records how the covenant people multiply and fill the land, each generation extending the promise. The Lord honors fruitfulness and presence in the land He gave.

Jabez was more honorable than his brothers—a stunning phrase that breaks through dry genealogy. His mother named him 'Jabez' meaning 'sorrow' because his birth brought her pain. Yet he did not remain defined by that sorrow. Sometimes our deepest wounds become the soil from which our greatest faith grows.

Jabez cried out to God: 'Bless me and enlarge my border. Let your hand be with me, and keep me from evil.' God answered. Here is bold prayer—not for riches or fame, but for blessing, for room to grow, for God's presence, and for protection from wrongdoing. The Lord delights when His children ask such things of Him, and He grants them.

Chelub, the brother of Shuhah, fathered Mehir, who fathered Eshton. The record continues, generation layered upon generation. Each link in the chain was a person who lived, loved, and built their own small corner of the great inheritance God was giving His people.

Eshton became father to cities—Beth Rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah. The men of Recah built places, established settlements, created homes where the covenant people could dwell and flourish. Building and settling are acts of faith in the Lord's promises.

The sons of Kenaz are recorded: Othniel and Seraiah. Othniel himself was a judge of Israel, known for his courage and his devotion to the Lord—and his family line carries that faithful witness into generations yet to come.

Seraiah became the father of Joab, father of the inhabitants of 'Ge Harashim'—the Valley of Craftsmen. They were artisans, workers of fine skill. The Lord honors honest work and skillful hands; He sees the carpenter, the weaver, the builder as much as the king and priest.

The sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh—this is Caleb the faithful spy, the one who stood with Joshua and believed the Lord's promise even when others doubted. His line continues, and his descendants inherit the blessing that flows from his faithfulness.
The sons of Jehallelel—Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria, and Asarel—each one named, each one part of the covenant people. The Lord's attention is not too small for the quiet branches of the family tree.

Ezrah fathered Jether and others through his wife, who bore Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah. Women who are named and honored for their fruitfulness remind us that the Lord values mothers and daughters as surely as sons.

Mered married Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh—a remarkable bridge between Egypt and Israel. She bore his children and gave them inheritance in the land of promise. Love and faithfulness sometimes cross borders the world would keep separate.

The wife of Hodiah—sister of Naham—fathered Keilah and Eshtemoa. Again, women appear in these genealogies, not merely as objects but as bearers and builders of the covenant line. Their names and work matter to the Lord's story.

The sons of Shimon—Amnon, Rinnah, Ben Hanan, and Tilon. The sons of Ishi—Zoheth and Ben Zoheth. Each line continues, each branch bears fruit. The Lord's covenant people grow and multiply, filling the land as He commanded.

The sons of Shelah include Er, Laadah, and the families of those who worked fine linen. Craftspeople, artisans, and workers are named and honored here—their callings and their handiwork matter in God's sight as much as any crown.

Jokim, the men of Cozeba, Joash, and Saraph—'these records are ancient.' The chronicler pauses to remind us that he is passing down an old memory, a lineage traced back through ages. What we inherit from faithful generations shapes what we pass on.

The potters of Netaim and Gederah lived and worked for the king. Their hands shaped clay; their labor served the kingdom. Even humble craftspeople—especially humble craftspeople—are part of God's design for order and flourishing.

Now the sons of Simeon are recorded: Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, and Shaul. One of the twelve tribes steps into view, their lineage preserved and honored. The Lord's covenant was made with all Israel; all are remembered in His sight.

Shallum, Mibsam, and Mishma—each son, each generation passing the name and blessing forward. Genealogies like this show us that the Lord builds His kingdom not through great events alone, but through the faithful, ordinary lives of His people across generations.
The sons of Mishma—Hammuel, Zaccur, Shimei. The line continues unbroken, each name a link in the chain the Lord is forging. Nothing that matters to God is ever forgotten.

Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters, yet his brothers did not multiply as much—nor did their families grow as large as Judah's. Here the chronicler notes a difference: some branches flourish more than others, yet all are counted among God's people. Fruitfulness is a blessing the Lord sovereignly bestows.

They dwelt at Beersheba, Moladah, Hazarshual—the places Simeon's people made their homes. Geography marks where faith took root, where families built their altars and their fields. The land itself becomes part of the covenant story.

Bilhah, Ezem, Tolad—more settlements of Simeon's line, each one a place where God's people dwelt and worshiped. The Lord's covenant people were not meant to be wanderers forever; they were called to possess and dwell in the land He promised.

Bethuel, Hormah, Ziklag—these cities housed the families of Simeon. Each place remembered, each settlement a sign that the Lord was fulfilling His promise to His people. They went from slavery to inheritance, from wandering to home.

Beth Marcaboth, Hazar Susim, Beth Biri, Shaaraim—these cities belonged to Simeon 'until the reign of David.' The chronicler marks a turning point: the land was theirs to dwell in, and then a great king arose to unite the kingdom. The Lord works through time and through chosen leaders.

Five more settlements—Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen, Ashan. The chronicler is thorough in listing Simeon's possession, reminding every generation where their inheritance lay. The Lord's faithfulness is specific and particular, not vague.

All their villages around the same cities extended to Baal. These were their settlements, and they had their genealogy—their place in the great record of God's covenant people. The Lord sees us not as isolated individuals but as part of a great family, woven into His eternal purpose.
Meshobab, Jamlech, Joshah—leaders of Simeon in a later age are named and honored. They too are part of the sacred record, remembered for their role in shepherding God's people.
Joel and others of Simeon's leaders are listed—Jehu, Joshibiah, Seraiah, Asiel. Each man named for his faithfulness and leadership. The Lord raises up shepherds for His flock in every generation.
Elioenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel, Benaiah—a full roster of leaders and faithful ones. Their names are preserved because they mattered to God and to His people in their time.

Ziza and his lineage—Shiphi, Allon, Jedaiah, Shimri, Shemaiah—are traced back through time. Here is continuity, a family line rooted deep in the history of God's people. Each name honors those who came before.

These men, mentioned by name, were princes in their families; their fathers' houses increased greatly. Leadership and blessing go together—as the Lord raises up shepherds, His people flourish. The growth of their families was itself a sign of God's favor.

They journeyed to the entrance of Gedor, to the east side of the valley, seeking pasture for their flocks. The people of Simeon were shepherds—they followed their herds to greener ground, always trusting God to provide. Sometimes faithfulness means simply going where the Lord leads.

They found good pasture—fat and abundant—and the land was wide, quiet, and peaceful. Those who had lived there before were descendants of Ham. The Lord gave them what they sought, and they dwelt in peace. His provision is both generous and good.

In the days of Hezekiah, these men struck the tents of the Meunim and destroyed them utterly, taking their place for pasture. The chronicler dates the event to a specific king—history is woven through the reign of known rulers. God's providence moves through the lives of both great and small, and all serve His purposes.

Five hundred of Simeon's sons, led by Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel, went to Mount Seir. They traveled far to secure their inheritance, led by men of courage and faithfulness. The Lord equips His people with leaders for the work they must do.

They struck the remnant of the Amalekites who escaped, and dwelt there to this day. Readers today hear an echo of God's faithfulness through all generations—the battles His people fought, the land they claimed, the legacy they built. We too inherit a story of deliverance and are called to faithfulness in our own time.

Here the scribe must tell an old, hard story: Reuben was born first, yet his own sin cost him what birthright means. Even a father's love cannot paper over that loss. Watch how the Lord honors faithfulness, not mere birth order.

Judah rose, and Joseph kept the birthright Reuben lost—yet the prince came from Judah's line. This is how the Lord works: He lifts up the faithful and weaves their place into His story, even when they started far behind.
Four sons named: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, Carmi—each a branch holding Reuben's name into the future. Names matter; generations matter. The Lord does not let faithfulness fade into silence.

Joel's line held the family priesthood through David's day. One name echoes down through a dozen: son, grandson, great-grandson—a ladder reaching from Joel all the way to Shemaiah. That's how God builds a people.
Micah, Reaiah, Baal—names strung together like beads on a thread, each one a person, each one known. The scribe takes time to honor them. So does the Lord, even names the world forgets.

Beerah was prince of Reuben when the Assyrian king dragged him away to captivity. A name spoken for all time, not to glorify him, but so the captivity is remembered—and so we remember that exile is real, and so is the faithfulness of those who faced it.

Jeiel and Zechariah were chieftains when the genealogy was reckoned. The scribe names them so history will know: these men held their tribes together, kept the records, guarded the memory of who they were.

Bela lived in Aroer, a real place east of the Jordan—from Nebo to Baal Meon, names on a map. The Lord knows where His people dwell, down to each town and well, just as He knows where you rest tonight.

They had room to spread—pasture reaching to the Euphrates itself. When God gives room, He gives it for a reason: to flourish, to multiply, to see His faithfulness overflow into generations. Gratitude is the only right answer to such plenty.
When Saul was king, the Reubenites fought the Hagrites and won—not because they were mightiest, but because they trusted. The Lord fights for those who call to Him first, before they fight.

Gad's sons camped across from Reuben, in Bashan's pastures all the way to Salecah. They lived facing one another, tribes in covenant, land held together in mutual trust. That's how God means for His people to dwell.

Joel, the chief; Shapham second; Janai and Shaphat below them—a chain of command, clear and humble. Leadership is not vanity; it's the willingness to serve a people faithfully and know your place in the line.

Seven brothers of their father's house, all named. Not one lost in the crowd. The scribe honors each: Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, Zia, Eber. Our God is a God of particulars, and so are His servants.
One long line of descent: father, grandfather, great-grandfather—Abihail, Huri, Jaroah, Gilead, Michael, Jeshishai, Jahdo, Buz, each one a link in the chain holding the people together across time.
Ahi was chief of their fathers' houses—the one who kept the trust, the one they came to when hard choices loomed. A faithful elder is worth more than gold.

Gilead in Bashan, its towns and the suburbs of Sharon—the geography is exact, named so no one would forget. The Lord's people live in a real land, with real places where He has put them down and called them home.

Jotham and Jeroboam—kings from a later age—verified the genealogy themselves. When rulers can say 'these records are true, these people are who they claim,' you know the record is weighty and the lineage real.

Forty-four thousand warriors, able to fight with bow and sword—the Lord counts them all. But number alone doesn't win wars; faith does. The number is recorded so we will see that even great strength serves under the Lord's command.

War with the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, Nodab—foes with real names, real plans. The Lord does not hide that His people faced enemies. He teaches us that faith is not escape from struggle, but trust through it.
They cried to God in battle, and He answered—the Hagrites fell. This is the Lord's pattern: when we call on Him, He hears, and He delivers. Not always without cost, but always faithfully.
Fifty thousand camels, two hundred fifty thousand sheep, two thousand donkeys—the spoils of victory, listed exactly. The Lord is not stingy with His blessings to those who trust Him.

Many fell, the war was of God—victory came not from might alone, but from the Lord's hand. Yet after, they rested in their place until captivity came. Even the victorious cannot escape exile if they turn from the Lord.
Half of Manasseh spread from Bashan to the high places—Baal Hermon, Senir, Mount Hermon, reaching to heaven itself. The Lord gave them room to grow, and they did, from one place to many.
Seven mighty men, famous for valor, heads of their houses—Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah, Jahdiel. A good name is better than great wealth, and the Lord remembers the righteous.

They played the prostitute after the gods of the peoples—a pattern we still hear echoed today. Readers in any age know the seduction of belonging to the world around us, the slow drift away from what we once held true. The Lord still calls us back.

Pul and Tilgath Pilneser carried them away—real kings, real exile, real loss. The Lord did not hide their failure or soften the cost. But He did not lose them either. Even in Gozan, He knew where they were.

Three sons—Gershon, Kohath, Merari—set the pattern for Levi's whole family line. From these three branches came all those who would keep the Tabernacle's service. What a gift, to come from a calling that runs this deep.

The Kohathites were the priestly branch, and look who stands here as the main trunk: Amram himself. His children would shake the world—Aaron the first high priest, Moses the lawgiver, Miriam the prophet.

Moses, Aaron, and Miriam—siblings who each carried their own calling, yet bound by the same redemptive story. Aaron's four sons begin the priestly succession, though two would stumble in the wilderness. The Lord makes all these names permanent here.
Watch the priesthood pass down through Eleazar's line, solid and steady. Phinehas steps into his father's office and becomes known for zeal—he runs toward the altar when others might flee.
Bukki and Uzzi—names that echo with faithful service, though we hear them only here. Yet the Lord kept them in His eye, generation to generation, priest after priest.

The priestly line marches on: Zerahiah to Meraioth, one hand passing to the next. This is what continuity looks like—not glamorous, but necessary, each man learning his father's trade of standing between God and His people.
Amariah, Ahitub—they come and go in the record, yet they held the line. When a man accepts the priesthood, he becomes a link in a chain meant to last forever.

Zadok appears here as the heir of a long priestly succession. He would become David's faithful high priest, a man so trustworthy that kings consulted him. The genealogy shows us his true pedigree: straight through Eleazar.
Ahimaaz becomes Zadok's heir, continuing a priesthood rooted in faithfulness. These aren't just names—they're links to men who bore the Urim and Thummim, who stood in the Holy Place.
Here Azariah performs the priesthood in Solomon's Temple—a pivotal note marking the shift from wilderness to a permanent house of prayer. After centuries of wandering, the worship finally settles.
The line continues unbroken into Solomon's era and beyond. Amariah and Ahitub—their names repeat (we've heard them before), yet they're new men in a new age. God's purposes span generations.
Zadok appears again—this branch of his line survives and prospers. A priest who kept his integrity through court intrigue and dynastic strife was rare and precious.
Hilkiah and Azariah—faithful men whose names echo through the kingdom's history. In the reforms to come, one of Hilkiah's descendants will discover the Book of the Law itself.
Seraiah and Jehozadak—the line stretches forward toward exile. Yet even here, the priesthood isn't broken; it continues in captivity and waits for restoration.

Jehozadak was carried away when Nebuchadnezzar conquered Jerusalem—yet this verse preserves his name and his priesthood survives the rupture. The exile is not the end; it is a pause in a story that resumes.
The record restarts the three sons of Levi—Gershom, Kohath, Merari. This time we'll hear from the singers and musicians, those who served not with the knife and censer but with voice and instrument.
Gershom's branch splits into Libni and Shimei. From these two lines came David's musicians—men like Asaph, whose songs still echo in our worship today.
The Kohathites are named again, now as the family from which singers arose. When David brought the ark to Jerusalem, it was Kohathites who sang and played.
The three families of Levi are bound by blood and calling—Mahli and Mushi of Merari, the youngest branch. Yet the Lord honored each family's gift for service.
Libni begins the descent through Gershom's line—Jahath, Zimmah, each man a link in the chain of worship. These aren't just ancestors; they're the roots of David's own singers.
The genealogy runs through Joah, Iddo, Zerah, Jeatherai—each one part of the Gershonite stream. How many of these men spent their whole lives learning and teaching the songs?
Now the Kohathites: Amminadab to Korah to Assir—lines within lines. Korah himself had a famous end (he rebelled in the wilderness), yet his descendants were honored to serve in song.
Elkanah appears here—the great-grandfather of Samuel, though we don't meet Samuel until later. Yet here he is, part of the music and worship of the Tabernacle.
Tahath, Uriel, Uzziah, Shaul—the Kohathite line continues. These men inherited the gift of song and the duty to shepherd Israel's worship.
Elkanah's sons—Amasai and Ahimoth—both musicians and servants. From Elkanah's line would come Samuel himself, the prophet-judge who would anoint Israel's kings.
Zophai and Nahath—Elkanah's descendants in the line of singers. Each name represents a man who carried the calling forward, though he may be remembered only in genealogy.
Eliab, Jeroham, Elkanah—the names compress generations into a handful of verses. Yet each one lived, loved, served, and passed the torch forward.

Samuel the prophet comes from this line of singers—Joel his father, Elkanah before that, all the way back to Kohath himself. A boy born in a barren woman's hope, a man who would reshape Israel's kingship.
Merari's branch—Mahli, Libni, Shimei, Uzzah—the third family of singers. These men stood ready to lift the music higher when David's heart was moved to praise.
Shimea, Haggiah, Asaiah—the Merarite line stretches forward, each man part of the music corps that would serve in Solomon's Temple and beyond.
After the ark came to rest—a turning point. David chose these singers and musicians to lead worship in the Tabernacle, not out of mere ceremony but from joy and reverence toward the Lord.
They sang and served through the Tent of Meeting's centuries, then transitioned into Solomon's Temple. Not a break in worship, but a deepening—a people learning to sing their faith to God.
Heman the singer emerges—a giant of Israel's music, descended from Samuel, crowned with wisdom by the Lord. Here is the culmination of the Kohathite singers, tracing back through generations.
The genealogy winds back: from Heman to Elkanah to Jeroham to Eliel—each link in the great chain that produces the chief musician of David's court.
Zuph, Elkanah, Mahath, Amasai—names in the shadow, yet they stood in the light once. Their faithfulness in obscurity bore fruit in Heman's great ministry.
The line spirals deeper into time: Elkanah, Joel, Azariah, Zephaniah—all funneling down to one man, Heman, who would become the voice of Israel's praise.
Tahath, Assir, Ebiasaph, Korah—the lineage passes through Korah, the rebel who perished in the wilderness, yet his descendants rose to sing in the very house Korah refused to serve.
Izhar, Kohath, Levi, Israel—the genealogy traces all the way back to the patriarchs, rooting Heman's gift in the family of the covenant itself.
Asaph stands on Heman's right hand—second among the singers, brother-in-service. His psalms fill the Psalter even today; his voice echoes across centuries of worship.
Michael, Baaseiah, Malchijah—Asaph's ancestors stretch backward, each one a note in the chord that produces this great musician.
Ethni, Zerah, Adaiah—the line continues back, branch after branch, all converging in Asaph's gift for music and prophecy.
Ethan, Zimmah, Shimei—the genealogy spirals deeper, showing how Asaph too descended from the singers of old, heir to a tradition as ancient as Levi himself.
Jahath, Gershom, Levi—Asaph's line traces back to the very roots. By blood and calling, he is Gershom's heir, a keeper of the family's sacred music.

Ethan of the Merarites stands on the left hand—a second great musician, descended from Merari's branch. Where Heman led from strength and Asaph from prophecy, Ethan offered the praise of the third family.
Hashabiah, Amaziah, Hilkiah—Ethan's ancestors reach back into Merari's line, each one part of the weaving that brings this master musician into being.
Amzi, Bani, Shemer—the Merarite stream flows on, carrying music and worship forward, generation to generation.
Mahli, Mushi, Merari, Levi—Ethan's line too traces back to the patriarchs, confirming that all three branches of Levite singers are rooted in the same deep covenant.
The other Levites served everywhere—carrying the Tabernacle, maintaining its rituals, keeping the house of God. Not all were singers; all were essential.
Aaron and his sons alone offered at the altars—the sacred boundary between priest and people, forever. The most holy work was theirs, atonement for Israel their calling.
Eleazar begins the restatement of Aaron's priestly line, a return to the theme of the chapter's opening. The priesthood and the music—twin streams of Levite service.
Phinehas, Abishua, Bukki, Uzzi, Zerahiah—the priestly succession flows on. Each priest was a custodian of atonement and intercession.
Meraioth, Amariah, Ahitub—more links in the high-priestly chain that stretched from Aaron through centuries of Israelite faith.
Zadok, Ahimaaz—Zadok we know as David's priest, a man of faithfulness and wisdom who never wavered. His son Ahimaaz served under him, carrying forward the priestly office.
Now the record turns to homes—the places where priests and Levites would dwell. The Lord didn't just give them calling; He gave them land, security, provision.
Hebron—the city of refuge and the center of Aaron's inheritance. How fitting: the city where David ruled, where wisdom gathered, became the priestly city.
Even the fields around Hebron went to Caleb, the faithful spy. A reminder that the priests weren't to own all the land—the Lord reserved portions for those who proved faithful in their own trials.
Cities of refuge—Hebron, Libnah, Jattir, Eshtemoa—places of mercy where the manslayer could flee. The priests lived where safety itself was sacred.
Hilen, Debir—each city a home for priestly families, each one an outpost of the Lord's mercy and order throughout Judah.
Ashan, Beth Shemesh—more cities where priests could settle and raise their children in the faith. The Lord didn't scatter them randomly but gave them real homes.
Thirteen cities for the Kohathites—a full inheritance scattered across Judah and Benjamin. The number thirteen reminds us the pattern extends throughout all Israel's tribes.
Ten cities given to the rest of the Kohathites from Manasseh—the Lord's provision extended beyond Judah's borders into the heartland.
The Gershomites received thirteen cities scattered across Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Bashan—the northern tribes blessed with priests in their midst to lead worship.
The Merarites received twelve cities—Reuben, Gad, Zebulun—again a pattern that shows the Lord distributed His servants throughout all Israel's landscape.
The people of Israel gave these cities to the Levites—not by compulsion but as part of the covenant's design, a voluntary sharing of inheritance with those who served the Lord.
Judah, Simeon, Benjamin—each tribe contributed cities where Levites would dwell and minister. Unity in worship required the whole people to support the servants of the altar.
Even the families of Kohath received portions in Ephraim—the central tribe, where wisdom and leadership often gathered. The priests weren't confined to Judah alone.
Shechem—a city heavy with history, where Jacob's sons once committed violence, where Joshua's covenant was renewed. Now it becomes a refuge city and a priestly dwelling.
Jokmeam, Beth Horon—cities known as military strongholds, now also centers of worship and priestly ministry. The Lord sanctified all of Israel's landscape.
Aijalon, Gath Rimmon—places that would see conflict and history, yet they remained priestly cities, refuges of grace amid the world's tumult.
Aner, Bileam in Manasseh—the Lord's provision extended to the half-tribe, ensuring the priestly family had secure places to worship and serve.
The Gershomites received Golan in Bashan—a city of refuge where the avenger's justice couldn't reach the innocent, guarded by priests who understood mercy.
Kedesh, Daberath in Issachar—each city a lighthouse of faith in the northern territories, where singers and servers kept the Lord's name alive.
Ramoth, Anem—more Gershonite settlements, scattered across the northern kingdom to ensure no corner of Israel lacked access to the priestly ministry and music.
From Asher came Mashal and Abdon—the western tribes too had their priestly cities, their sanctuaries of worship where the Lord was known and served.
Hukok, Rehob—more Asherite cities, each one a seed of faith planted in the soil of Israel's inheritance.
Kedesh in Galilee—famous as a city of refuge, its location in the North strategized for justice. Here Gershonites ensured the Lord's sanctuary extended even to the far reaches.
The Merarites received Rimmon and Tabor in Zebulun—mountain and plains, each city a place where the third family of Levites could build their homes.
Beyond the Jordan—even the Trans-Jordan tribes, Reuben and Gad, received Merarite cities. Bezer was another city of refuge, where the Lord's mercy reached across the river.
Kedemoth, Mephaath—Reubenite cities now devoted to priests and Levites, extending the reach of worship across the Jordan's eastern bank.
Ramoth in Gilead—the great city east of Jordan, a fortress city of refuge, now also a beacon of priestly service in Gad's territory.
Heshbon, Jazer—the final cities listed, completing a map of mercy and worship that spans all Israel from north to south, west to east. The priests lived where they were needed most.

The sons of Issachar are named first—Tola, Puah, Jashub, Shimron. Four brothers, four lines of blessing branching out. It strikes me that the recorder noticed them all, gave each a name that would echo through generations.
Tola's line produced twenty-two thousand six hundred mighty men by David's day—strength multiplied through faithfulness. The Lord loves to take one faithful person's legacy and make it a multitude.
Five sons to Izrahiah, all chiefs. The text marks them as leaders—not by accident, but by the Lord's design. A father watches his children step into responsibility and sees the hand of God at work.

Thirty-six thousand warriors, because "they had many wives and sons." The blessing of a full house, a thriving line. The Lord fills what He ordains, and abundance flows through generations when family is treasured.

Eighty-seven thousand total—Issachar's whole roll listed by genealogy. Not forgotten, not lost in the crowd. Every name written down, every line accounted for. The God who knows the stars by name knows us too.
Benjamin's three sons begin now—Bela, Becher, Jediael. Three branches from one strong trunk. Even in a genealogy, you feel the family tree growing, each generation another layer of roots and fruit.
Bela's line produced twenty-two thousand thirty-four warriors—"mighty men of valor." Courage is a legacy that runs in families, drawn up from faith deeper than the grave.

Nine sons to Becher, each name distinct: Zemirah, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jeremoth, Abijah, Anathoth, Alemeth. Nine voices, nine choices, nine chances to bring honor or shame to the house. The Lord sees each one.

Twenty thousand two hundred mighty men from Becher's house. When faithfulness runs through a line unbroken, it multiplies in strength—not by conquest, but by the blessing of the Lord who holds all generations in His hand.

Jediael's son Bilhan, and Bilhan's seven sons—Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tarshish, Ahishahar. Generations flowing onward, names preserved, stories carried forward by those who came after.
Seventeen thousand two hundred warriors, able to march to war. Behind every number stands a person—a son, a father, a man who stood firm when faithfulness was tested.
Shuppim, Huppim, the sons of Ir, Hushim, the sons of Aher—names we scarce know, yet the chronicler wrote them all. The Lord's memory is perfect; no faithful servant is ever truly forgotten.

Naphtali's sons: Jahziel, Guni, Jezer, Shallum, and the sons of Bilhah—the maidservant's children carried forward through generations. The Lord lifted up the lowly and made them a people; no birth is beneath His notice or care.

Manasseh's son Asriel, born of an Aramean concubine. And Machir—he became the father of Gilead, whose very name would mark a place of balm, of healing. Sometimes the Lord writes a legacy in geography, in the land itself.

Machir took a wife and built a house. Zelophehad is named—a man whose daughters would one day go before the Lord seeking their inheritance, teaching Israel that the Lord honors the courageous plea for justice.

Maacah bore Peresh and Sheresh, and their sons Ulam and Rakem. A mother's name preserved forever alongside her sons'—the Lord sees the woman who bears and raises up the next generation with quiet faith.
Bedan, son of Ulam—the line continues, each generation a link in an unbroken chain stretching back to Jacob and forward to God's purpose. We are never alone; we inherit the faith of those before us.

Hammolecheth, sister and mother to Ishhod, Abiezer, Mahlah. Her sons bore great names—Abiezer the mighty, names that speak of God's help. A sister's blessing flows through generations she will never see.
Shemida's four sons: Ahian, Shechem, Likhi, Aniam. Shechem—a place and a name, rooted deep in Israel's story. The Lord writes history through families, weaves lives into the very land.

Ephraim's line opens: Shuthelah, then Bered, Tahath, Eleadah, Tahath again—generations traced careful and complete. Each name a heartbeat in the great story of Israel's survival and God's faithfulness.

Ezer and Elead, killed by men of Gath for cattle. Tragedy strikes even within the people of God—theft, violence, sons cut down in their youth. Yet the Lord's story does not end in death; it ends in Him.
Ephraim mourned many days for his slain sons. His brothers came to comfort him—a picture of the body grieving, standing with one another in loss. Jesus wept; so do His people, and so can we.

Then Ephraim conceived again, named his new son Beriah—"because there was trouble with his house." From sorrow comes another son, another chance, another mercy. The Lord turns mourning into His strange comfort.

His daughter Sheerah built Beth Horon the lower and upper, and Uzzen Sheerah. A woman's work in stone, her engineering skill recorded alongside the men's. The Lord delights to see His daughters build, strengthen, leave a mark on the land.
Rephah, Resheph, Telah, Tahan—the line branches again through generations. Each father names his son, each son becomes a father in turn, the covenant passed forward like a torch through the darkness.
Ladan, Ammihud, Elishama—Elishama's name speaks of God hearing. In names, Israel testified: the Lord hears our cry, sees our plight, remembers us. That same God hears His people still.

Nun, and his son Joshua. There it is—the great Joshua, who led Israel into the promised land, springs from this line. One man's faithfulness shaped a nation's crossing; the Lord crowns with honor those who serve Him wholly.

Bethel, Naaran, Gezer, Shechem, Azzah—the land itself held by Ephraim. These towns map the territory promised, settled, held by faith. Geography becomes theology when we see the Lord's faithfulness written across the earth.

Beth Shean, Taanach, Megiddo, Dor—ancient strongholds, places where Israel's story unfolded. "The children of Joseph lived in these." The God who promised the land brought them safe to its fulfillment.

Asher's four sons and a sister: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, Serah. Serah named alongside the brothers—the chronicler was careful to mark her. She belonged fully to the people, counted as one of them.
Beriah's sons: Heber and Malchiel, Malchiel the father of Birzaith. The genealogy grows dense now, but each name tells of lives lived, choices made, blessings given and received.
Heber fathered Japhlet, Shomer, Hotham, and their sister Shua. Four siblings, one family bearing the name forward. The Lord loves to see families knit together in love and faithfulness.
Japhlet's sons: Pasach, Bimhal, Ashvath. Three more branches, three more sets of descendants who would inherit the faith of their fathers and pass it on or set it aside.

Shemer's sons: Ahi, Rohgah, Jehubbah, Aram. Four names, and in each a story the recorder thought worth keeping. Not all deeds are recorded in Scripture, but none are forgotten by the One who knows all.
Helem's sons: Zophah, Imna, Shelesh, Amal. Four more branches of the great tree, each one tender with possibility, each one held in the hand of the God who ordained them.
Zophah's many sons: Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, Imrah, Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran, Beera—a great flock of children, each one precious, each one known by name to the Lord who formed them.
Jether's sons: Jephunneh, Pispa, Ara. Three more, the line continuing, generation after generation in an endless chain reaching toward eternity.
Ulla's sons: Arah, Hanniel, Rizia. Three more voices, three more names pressed into the page by the chronicler's careful hand, as if to say: they mattered, and God remembers.

"All these were the children of Asher...twenty-six thousand men." Readers today hear an echo in these genealogies: we too are numbered, known by the Father, counted among His people. We don't just survive—we thrive, multiplying in faithful generations as we trust in Him.

Benjamin's sons begin a whole lineage of the faithful remnant. Notice the order—each name a thread held tight by the God who promised never to leave His people without a voice. These are the ones who would anchor Judah's return.

Nohah and Rapha complete Benjamin's immediate sons—the fourth and fifth branches. I see in genealogies like this that God counts every name, every generation. None are forgotten, even when the world thought the line was broken.

Bela's children—Addar, Gera, Abihud—extend the family further. Each generation builds on the faithfulness of the last, a living chain of covenant people. The Lord was weaving His purpose through Benjamin long before the exile, and never let the thread snap.

Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah—more descendants, more proof that God's people multiply and spread. Even in a list of names, I sense the quiet miracle: God preserved His people when it looked like all would be lost.

Gera, Shephuphan, and Huram close Bela's line. I've always loved how the Chronicler keeps naming—it's a song of remembrance, a way of saying, 'You matter to God, and we won't let you disappear from the story.' Exile could scatter people, but not memory in God's hands.

Ehud's sons became heads of families in Geba and were carried captive to Manahath—a hard naming of deportation, yet the record survives. Even exile is held in God's memory, and those scattered are never erased from His book.

Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera led the captivity—and yet they became fathers themselves, Uzza and Ahihud following after. What strikes me is that captors and captives both live on in God's plan, and both are named. Nothing is wasted in His sight.

Shaharaim sent away his wives Hushim and Baara, then fathered children in the field of Moab—a life fractured and strange, yet still held in the genealogy. I see in this hard honesty that God's record doesn't hide broken families; it keeps them whole in His memory.

By Hodesh, Shaharaim fathered Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam—a new beginning, a new wife, more sons. Life moved on even in exile, even in loss. God's mercy flows through our worst seasons, giving new names and new chances to those who belong to Him.

Jeuz, Shachia, Mirmah—Shaharaim's sons who became heads of households. Even in displacement, leadership remained, and families held their shape. I see the Lord's hand keeping His people organized and purposeful, no matter the storm.

Hushim's children were Abitub and Elpaal—another wife, another line carried forward. The genealogy doesn't hide the complexity of a life split across wives and exile, but includes it. God's love meets us where we actually are, however tangled the path.

Elpaal's sons Eber and Misham—and Shemed who built Ono and Lod. Here builders emerge from exile, people who took rubble and made towns again. I see in this that God grants His people not only survival but the grace to rebuild what was lost.

Beriah and Shema were heads of fathers' households in Aijalon, and they put to flight the inhabitants of Gath—a rare glimpse of military prowess, a reminder that even after exile, God's people could stand and resist. Weakness is never the Lord's final word.

Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth—more sons, more branches spreading. I notice the genealogy keeps listing without apology or summary; each name is a thread, and the whole pattern is what matters. God doesn't compress His people down; He preserves their multitude.

Zebadiah, Arad, Eder—three more, each real to the Lord, each counted. I've learned that God's arithmetic isn't about grand totals; it's about knowing each face, each name. These lists remind me that I'm never one of millions to Him—I'm known by name.

Michael, Ishpah, Joha—Beriah's descendants continuing the line. The Lord weaves families through generations like a craftsman with thread, each color distinct yet part of one whole. Beriah's branch reached deep into Benjamin's restored settlement.

Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hizki, Heber—Elpaal's line carries forward, each name a link to the covenant. What strikes me is that these genealogies span captivity and return; they're proof that exile didn't end the story—God's purpose ran right through it.

Ishmerai, Izliah, Jobab—more of Elpaal's sons, building the family tree through remembered names. I've come to treasure how these lists honor each person, not as a footnote but as someone whose life mattered to God's plan.

Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi—another cluster of names, another household. The Lord built His people back not as one mass but as families, each with its own story and place. That's how grace works—restoring us not in theory but in real relationships.

Elienai, Zillethai, Eliel—yet more children, yet more proof that the remnant was alive and fruitful. I see the Lord's blessing in every name, in the sheer fact that Benjamin didn't disappear but flourished, bearing children even after exile.

Adaiah, Beraiah, Shimrath—Shimei's sons, another branch of the family taking shape. I notice the genealogy doesn't rush through these names; each is given time to exist, to be known. That's how God treats His people: with unhurried, personal attention.

Ishpan, Eber, Eliel—more sons of Shimei, extending the line. I've noticed that in these genealogies, the Lord preserves not just the famous but the faithful faithful, the ones who quietly held the faith through exile and built again.

Abdon, Zichri, Hanan—three more names in a long chain. What I treasure here is that God's commitment to His people wasn't conditional on their wealth or fame; it was absolute, written in genealogies that survive empires.

Hananiah, Elam, Anthothijah—still more sons, still more families. I see in the length of these lists that God delights in abundance, in the fruitfulness of His people even when the world called them defeated. Our God is a God of multiplication.

Iphdeiah, Penuel—Shashak's descendants, another branch rooting itself back into the promised land. I'm moved by how the genealogy keeps building, name after name, as if to say, 'See? The Lord never abandoned His people. Here they are, alive and remembered.'

Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah—more of Shashak's line, keeping the family rooted. There's something deeply comforting about being included in a genealogy, about knowing your name will outlast kingdoms. That's what the Lord offers His people.

Jaareshiah, Elijah, Zichri—and Jeroham's sons as well. I notice these weren't the kings or prophets we'd expect to hear; they were ordinary faithful who held the line and kept covenant. The Lord honors obscurity that trusts Him.

These chiefs lived in Jerusalem—the moment the genealogy surfaces from names into place. After exile, Benjamin's leaders returned and took their place in the holy city again, heads of households, restoring community. God's promise to gather His people came true.

The father of Gibeon lived there with his wife Maacah—now we move to a specific household in a specific place. Gibeon wasn't the center of power, but it mattered, and the genealogy marks it. The Lord cares about every settlement, every family.

Abdon his firstborn, then Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab—five sons built this household. I see in Kish's name a connection forward (he would father Saul), but here he's simply one of five, one part of a beloved family. The Lord lifts up the humble.

Gedor, Ahio, Zecher—three more sons, completing the count of Gibeon's house. I notice the genealogy keeps the family intact, naming them all, making clear that each child was known and loved. God builds His kingdom through real families, not abstractions.

Mikloth became the father of Shimeah, and they lived near their brothers in Jerusalem—family staying close, bonds held tight. I've learned that one of God's deepest gifts is kinship, the chance to live near those who share your faith and story.

Ner became the father of Kish, Kish of Saul, Saul of Jonathan—here the genealogy names the first king of Israel, and his son, Jonathan, whose loyalty to God ran deeper than to dynasty. One moment the line is obscure Benjamites, the next it touches royalty.

Jonathan's son was Merib Baal, and Merib Baal fathered Micah—the royal line continues through the exile, though now hidden, no longer on a throne. Even displaced, God's people carry purpose; even in loss, there's a hidden kingship that belongs to Christ.

Micah's sons—Pithon, Melech, Tarea, Ahaz—the line extends into obscurity, names that belong now to descendants unnamed in the narrative. This is where genealogies lead: to people who served the Lord in complete silence, known only to Him.

Ahaz fathered Jehoaddah, who fathered Alemeth, Azmaveth, and Zimri—and Zimri fathered Moza. I see how deeply the genealogy runs, tracing bloodlines through generations of exile and return. Not one name was forgotten in God's reckoning.

Moza fathered Binea, Raphah, Eleasah, Azel—the line continues deeper still, each generation a link to the promise. I'm struck by the Lord's faithfulness: even when His people seemed forgotten, He held the thread of their covenant steady.

Azel had six sons—Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, Hanan—a full household, a branch bearing fruit. Even at the end of the genealogy's deep reach, we see God's blessing: families, names, purpose, all held in His hands.

Eshek's brother had sons—Ulam the firstborn, Jeush, Eliphelet—another household, another testament to God's covenant enduring. These names will never be famous, yet here they are, written forever in Israel's genealogy, in the record of God's faithfulness.

Ulam's sons were mighty men of valor, archers with many descendants—one hundred fifty. Readers today hear an echo: strength doesn't come from prominence but from trust in the God who names us and holds us. Benjamin's lineage carried the sacred trust through exile to restoration, and we still bear witness to that faithfulness. As of 2026-10, I see in this the Lord's promise: my name, too, is written in a genealogy that will outlast empires.

All Israel listed by genealogy, all the way back. Then the hard truth—Judah taken captive to Babylon for disobedience. Even in exile, the Lord does not abandon His people; He marks each name, remembering.
After exile, the first to settle back in their own cities were Israel, priests, Levites, and temple servants. Not the powerful first—the faithful ones, ready to rebuild what was broken.
Jerusalem draws them back: Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, Manasseh—tribes separated long ago now living side by side again. The Lord gathers His scattered children home.
Uthai returns, a name anchored in generations. He carries his lineage forward—a man known by his fathers, stepping back into the land his grandfathers held.
Asaiah and the Shilonites—Shiloh once held the ark of God, the place where Samuel heard the Lord's voice. Now these men return to serve in a rebuilt Jerusalem.
Six hundred ninety souls from Zerah's line. The Lord counts each one; every name, every family matters to Him in this great return.
The sons of Benjamin settling in Jerusalem. Once divided from their brothers, now dwelling in the same city, faithful to the God who calls them home.
More Benjamites named—Ibneiah, Elah, Meshullam, each a head of a household. The Lord rebuilds His people family by family, name by name, in patient love.
Nine hundred fifty-six men, all heads of fathers' households. Each one carries responsibility for his family and their place in the restored covenant community.
The priests return: Jedaiah, Jehoiarib, Jachin—names that reach back to Aaron himself. The altar calls them home to serve again in the house of God.
Azariah the son of Hilkiah, ruler of God's house. The high priest returns to oversee the sacred work—not a position of worldly power, but of service to the Most High.
More priests listed—Adaiah, Maasai—each with their own genealogy, their own priestly line. The Lord restores His priesthood to minister before Him.
One thousand seven hundred sixty priests, very able men for God's service. Not chosen for their strength, but equipped by God for the work of His house.
Shemaiah the Levite, of the sons of Merari. The Levites return to their calling—to support and sustain the worship of God in His dwelling place.
Bakbakkar, Heresh, Galal, Mattaniah—Levites whose names declare God's faithfulness. Each one finds their place in the restored work of praise and service.
Obadiah serves the Lord; Berechiah, whose name means 'the Lord blesses,' lives in the villages around Jerusalem. Even the suburbs become sacred space when the faithful dwell there.
The porters at the gates: Shallum, Akkub, Talmon, Ahiman. They guard the threshold of God's house—a humble but holy trust, standing watch over the holy place.
The king's gate eastward—the ancient post where once watchmen served the kingdom. Now these porters serve Yahweh in the camp of the Levites, faithful to a higher kingdom.
Shallum the Korahite bears a name of an ancient lineage—his fathers kept the entry to Yahweh's camp in the wilderness. He continues their trust in a new generation, guarding the sacred threshold.

Phinehas the son of Eleazar was ruler over them in time past—a priest of old who turned back God's wrath with covenant zeal. His memory stands as a sign that the Lord rewards faithfulness with leadership.
Zechariah the son of Meshelemiah, porter of the door of the Tent of Meeting. Standing at the entrance—a place where heaven and earth touch, where holiness meets those who enter.
Two hundred twelve porters, chosen and listed by David and Samuel the seer, ordained in an office of trust. The Lord uses His servant leaders to establish faithful guardians of His house.
The porters and their children watch the gates of God's house by wards—not a passing duty but a stewardship handed down through generations, standing watch over the place where the Lord dwells.
Four sides guarded: east, west, north, south. The Lord's house watched from every direction, kept safe by faithful hands stationed all around it.
Every seven days the village brothers come in to take their turn at the gates. The whole community shares the watch—each tribe, each family bearing their part of this sacred trust.
Four chief porters in office of trust, watching the treasuries and rooms of God's house. To be trusted with God's treasures—what a humbling calling, what an honor.
They stayed around God's house day and night, their duty on them like a sacred mantle. The morning opens the gates—and the faithful are already there, ready to serve.
Vessels brought in by count, taken out by count—the careful tending of holy things. Even in small details, the Lord calls us to faithfulness and order.

Furniture, vessels, flour, wine, oil, frankincense, spices—all appointed to faithful hands. Each item carries meaning: bread for hunger, oil for anointing, incense for prayer. The Lord's house lacks nothing.
The priests prepare the mixing of spices—an art passed down, a craft by which holy worship is sweetened. Faithfulness shows itself in the smallest acts of care.
Mattithiah, firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, has oversight of the baked goods. Bread from the oven—the sustenance that fed the priests and the people, made with trust and order.
The Kohathites prepare the show bread every Sabbath—twelve loaves set before the Lord. A sign of covenant, of God's presence, kept alive by faithful hands week after week.
The singers, heads of households living in the temple rooms, employed day and night. They lift their voices in praise—the sound of worship rising continually before the throne of God.
These are the chief men, heads of fathers' households, throughout their generations. In Jerusalem they dwell—pillars of the restored community, faithful leaders whose families anchor God's people.
Jeiel the father of Gibeon, living in the city he founded with his wife Maacah. A household rooted and stable, ready to build and tend what God has restored.
Abdon, Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab—six sons named, each bearing his place in the family line. The Lord blesses faithful homes with many to carry on the work.
Gedor, Ahio, Zechariah, Mikloth—four more sons, the household full and fruitful. A large family speaks of God's blessing in the restored land.
Mikloth becomes a father himself, and all his line dwells in Jerusalem near their brothers. The generations continue—each one birthing the next, the covenant unbroken.
Ner, Kish, Saul—kings from this line. The genealogy traces toward David, toward the one who will sit on the throne of God forever. Even in genealogy, the way of the Lord becomes clear.
Jonathan the son of Saul had a son, Merib Baal. A bridge between the old king and the new; the line continues though the kingdom changed hands.
The sons of Micah: Pithon, Melech, Tahrea, Ahaz. Each name a child, each child a bearer of blessing into the future that God holds in His hand.
Ahaz, Jarah, Alemeth, Azmaveth, Zimri—names strung like beads on a cord, one generation giving birth to the next. The chain of covenant runs unbroken through time.
Moza, Binea, Rephaiah, Eleasah, Azel—the line deepens and branches, each son a promise kept, each name a child known by God.

Azel had six sons whose names are remembered—Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah, Hanan. Readers today hear an echo in this careful recording: the Lord knows each one. Every name matters to Him. Nothing is forgotten in His sight.
The battle turns against Israel on that slope—and we see again what the prophets warned. When we run from the Lord's throne, we're left standing alone before our enemies.
Saul's sons fall at Gilboa—the next generation pays a steep price for the father's refusal to listen. A kingdom divided against its own God cannot hold its children safe.
The archers close in, and Saul's fear overtakes him. He has ruled for decades, yet in the hour of trial, no armor guards a heart that never sought the One who truly shields us.

Saul asks his armor-bearer to end his life rather than face capture. How far a king can fall—from leading God's people to taking his own sword. Even in despair, the Lord's grace is never locked away; Saul simply never knocked.
The armor-bearer follows his king into death—loyalty twisted into mutual ruin. How often we follow those we trust into the dark, not knowing we ourselves might choose a different path.
Saul's whole house falls together. A tragic end for a man who once held such promise—anointed by a prophet, chosen by the people—undone by pride and a stiffened neck.
When the soldiers see their king is gone, they scatter—and the land falls to the enemy. A kingdom without a true shepherd soon becomes prey.
The Philistines find Saul sprawled on the slope where he fell. How different his end from what a king anointed by God's own prophet might have imagined.

They parade Saul's head and armor through the pagan cities, broadcasting victory to stone and wood idols. A humiliation meant to prove the gods of Philistia stronger—yet their idols were always nothing but dust and pride.
Saul's armor hangs in a pagan shrine, and his head is fixed in the temple of Dagon—desecration meant as the final word. But the Lord's word had already been spoken long before.
News reaches Jabesh Gilead, where Saul once showed mercy early in his reign. Now the city hears only that their king lies broken on an enemy shrine.
The brave men of Jabesh risk everything to retrieve Saul's body and his sons'—they fast seven days in grief. Even in shame, there is kindness; even in silence, there are those who remember and honor.

The chronicler speaks plainly: Saul died for his unfaithfulness—he would not keep the Lord's word, and he sought a medium instead. When we turn away from the true God, all our other decisions crumble.

In Saul's end, readers today hear an echo: the Lord does not cling to the unwilling. He took the kingdom from Saul and gave it to David—and in that shift lies a mercy Saul never grasped. God was always moving toward a heart that would follow.

All Israel gathers to David at Hebron, saying 'we are your bone and your flesh.' There's a tender recognition here—they see him not as a distant ruler, but as kin. The Lord draws a scattered people together around one shepherd.

The people recall that even under Saul, David was the real shepherd—he led out and brought in Israel. They cite Yahweh's word to David: shepherd and prince. The Lord's claim on us often comes before the world sees it.

All the elders come to Hebron and make covenant with David before Yahweh, then anoint him king—fulfilling Samuel's anointing years before. Covenant-making in God's sight seals what has long been promised.

David and all Israel go to Jerusalem (Jebus), where the Jebusites still hold the city. To take the seat of kingship, he must enter the enemy's stronghold. Sometimes the Lord's calling takes us into places we must contest in faith.
The Jebusites boast: 'You will not come in here.' But David takes the stronghold of Zion. What seemed impossible falls when we move in the Lord's name—and becomes known ever after as David's city.

David offers chief command to whoever strikes the Jebusites first. Joab rises first and is made chief. Sometimes honor goes to the one willing to lead—to step first through the breach, not wait for a safer path.
